blocks.title: De Rham's theorem
blocks.body:
De Rham proved in 1931 that integration identifies the groups on this page with real singular cohomology. To state this we need cohomology on the singular side. For a space $X$, the real singular cochains are $C^k(X;\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{Hom}(C_k(X),\mathbb{R})$ with coboundary $(\delta\lambda)(\sigma)=\lambda(\partial\sigma)$, and $H^k(X;\mathbb{R})$ is the cohomology of this complex (Ginory, Definitions 3.1 to 3.3). Because $\mathbb{R}$ is a field, the universal coefficient theorem reduces to
$$H^k(X;\mathbb{R})\cong\operatorname{Hom}\big(H_k(X),\mathbb{R}\big),\qquad[\lambda]\mapsto\big([c]\mapsto\lambda(c)\big),$$
and Chua simply takes the right side as the definition. Singular cohomology inherits from [[homology]] functoriality, homotopy invariance and a Mayer–Vietoris sequence for open covers (dualise the homology sequence; $\operatorname{Hom}(-,\mathbb{R})$ preserves exactness).

To integrate we need smooth chains. Let $H_k^\infty(M)$ be the homology of the smooth chain complex $C^\infty_*(M)$ from the section on integration.

blocks.title: Smooth chains suffice
blocks.body: The inclusion $C^\infty_*(M)\subseteq C_*(M)$ induces isomorphisms $H^\infty_k(M)\cong H_k(M)$ for all $k$. Proof not given here: see Ginory, Theorem 4.4 (each simplex is joined to a smooth one by a homotopy compatible with faces, built inductively with the Whitney approximation theorem, and prism operators give the chain homotopy), or Lee, Chapter 18, cited by Petrov as Theorem 18.7.

blocks.title: The de Rham homomorphism
blocks.body:
For a closed $k$-form $\omega$ define
$$I[\omega]\in H^k(M;\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R}),\qquad I[\omega]\big([c]\big)=\int_{c}\omega,$$
where $c$ is a smooth cycle representing the class (possible by the previous theorem). It is well defined by Stokes, exactly as for periods: exact forms integrate to $0$ on cycles and closed forms integrate to $0$ on boundaries. It is natural, $I\circ F^*=F^*\circ I$ for smooth $F$, because $\int_{F\circ\sigma}\omega=\int_\sigma F^*\omega$.

In words: a de Rham class is turned into the function "integrate over this cycle".

blocks.title: De Rham's theorem
blocks.body: For every smooth manifold $M$ and every $k$, the de Rham homomorphism $I:H^k(M)\to H^k(M;\mathbb{R})$ is an isomorphism. It is natural in $M$, and it carries the wedge product to the cup product, so it is an isomorphism of graded rings. Consequently de Rham cohomology is a topological (indeed homotopy) invariant: homeomorphic manifolds have isomorphic de Rham cohomology rings.

We follow the argument that Petrov and Ginory take from Lee, who credits it to Bredon; Chua outlines the same steps. Call $M$ a de Rham manifold if $I$ is an isomorphism in every degree, and call an open cover a de Rham cover if every finite intersection of its members is a de Rham manifold. The multiplicativity is not proved here; Chua and Wikipedia state it, and it is not needed for the dimension statements used on this page.

Step 0: compatibility with Mayer–Vietoris. For $M=U\cup V$, the integration maps for $U$, $V$, $U\cap V$, $M$ form a map from the de Rham Mayer–Vietoris sequence to the singular one. The squares involving restrictions commute by naturality. The square with the connecting maps commutes too; this is a direct check with the formula for $\delta$ and a decomposition of cycles into $U$-small and $V$-small pieces, done in Petrov, Proposition 5.3(b), and in Lee, Chapter 18. We take it from there.

Step 1: convex open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are de Rham. For $k\ge1$ both sides vanish (Poincaré lemma; contractible spaces have the homology of a point). For $k=0$ both sides are $\mathbb{R}$, and $I$ sends the constant function $1$ to the functional taking the value $1$ on the class of a point, which is nonzero.

Step 2: disjoint unions. If $M=\bigsqcup_jM_j$ with each $M_j$ de Rham, then both sides are products over $j$ (for singular cohomology, $H_k(M)=\bigoplus_jH_k(M_j)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(\bigoplus,\mathbb{R})=\prod\operatorname{Hom}$), and $I$ is the product of the $I_j$.

Step 3: finite de Rham covers. If $U$, $V$ and $U\cap V$ are de Rham, the ladder of the two Mayer–Vietoris sequences (the figure in the duality section, with $\Phi=I$) and the five lemma show that $U\cup V$ is de Rham. By induction on the number of sets, a manifold with a finite de Rham cover is de Rham: for $U_1,\dots,U_{p+1}$, put $U=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_p$ and $V=U_{p+1}$; then $U$ and $U\cap V$ have de Rham covers of $p$ sets.

Step 4: de Rham bases. Suppose $M$ has a de Rham cover that is a basis of its topology. Choose a smooth proper exhaustion function $f:M\to[0,\infty)$ and set $A_m=f^{-1}([m,m+1])$ (compact) and $A'_m=f^{-1}\big((m-\tfrac12,m+\tfrac32)\big)$. Cover $A_m$ by finitely many basis sets inside $A'_m$ and let $B_m$ be their union; it is covered by finitely many basis sets, all of whose finite intersections are de Rham by assumption, so $B_m$ is de Rham by Step 3. Since $B_m\subseteq A'_m$, $B_m$ meets only $B_{m-1}$ and $B_{m+1}$. Let $U=\bigcup_{m\text{ odd}}B_m$ and $V=\bigcup_{m\text{ even}}B_m$. Each is a disjoint union of de Rham manifolds, hence de Rham by Step 2, and $U\cap V=\bigsqcup_m(B_m\cap B_{m+1})$ is a disjoint union of manifolds with finite de Rham covers (by the pairwise intersections of the chosen basis sets), hence de Rham. Step 3 applied to $M=U\cup V$ finishes this step.

Step 5: open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ have the basis of convex balls, and finite intersections of convex sets are convex, so by Steps 1 and 4 they are de Rham. Every manifold has a basis consisting of open sets diffeomorphic to open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (chart domains), whose finite intersections are again of that kind, so Step 4 applies to every manifold.

blocks.title: Why de Rham cohomology equals real singular cohomology
blocks.body: The theorem has several proofs, and papers cite whichever matches their tools.

items.label: Integration and induction
items.body: The proof above: integration over smooth chains is a natural map; it is an isomorphism on convex sets by the two Poincaré lemmas, and Mayer–Vietoris with the five lemma spreads it to finite covers, then (using an exhaustion function) to all manifolds.

items.label: Fine resolutions of sheaves
items.body: Lim (Theorem 2.2) compares two resolutions of the constant sheaf $\mathbb{R}$: by sheaves of smooth forms and by sheaves of smooth singular cochains. Both are acyclic (fine or soft), so both compute sheaf cohomology $H^*(M;\mathbb{R})$. Wikipedia presents the forms side the same way, with the Poincaré lemma giving exactness of the resolution and partitions of unity giving fineness.

items.label: Čech cohomology of a good cover
items.body: For a good cover, de Rham cohomology agrees with the Čech cohomology of the cover with real coefficients, which depends only on the combinatorics of which sets meet (the nerve). Wikipedia credits this version essentially to Weil (1952); Bott–Tu build it from the Čech–de Rham double complex, and Guillemin–Haine sketch it in §5.8.

items.label: Currents
items.body: Allowing forms with distributional coefficients (currents) gives a complex that also computes singular cohomology and contains chains themselves as currents of integration. The price is the product: currents cannot in general be multiplied, so this version does not see the ring structure.

blocks.title: Periods determine classes
blocks.body: A closed $k$-form $\omega$ on $M$ is exact if and only if $\int_z\omega=0$ for every smooth $k$-cycle $z$. More generally, the integration pairing $H^k(M)\times H_k(M;\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}$ is perfect when $H_k(M;\mathbb{R})$ is finite dimensional, and for $k=1$ the criterion says that a closed $1$-form has a potential if and only if its line integrals around all closed loops vanish.

If all periods vanish, $I[\omega]=0$ as an element of $\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R})$; by injectivity of $I$, $[\omega]=0$. The converse is Stokes. For the perfect pairing: $H^k(M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{R}}(H_k(M;\mathbb{R}),\mathbb{R})$, which is the dual space. For $k=1$, every $1$-cycle is homologous to a sum of closed loops, which can be taken smooth.

blocks.title: Torsion is invisible: the Klein bottle and the projective plane
blocks.body: Using the integral homology computed on [[homology]], $H_1(K)\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2(K)=0$ for the Klein bottle and $H_1(\mathbb{RP}^2)=\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2(\mathbb{RP}^2)=0$, compute their de Rham cohomology, and explain why a closed form has zero integral over a cycle $c$ with $2c$ a boundary.
blocks.solution: By de Rham's theorem $H^k_{dR}=\operatorname{Hom}(H_k,\mathbb{R})$, and every homomorphism from a finite group to $\mathbb{R}$ is zero. So for the Klein bottle $H^0=\mathbb{R}$, $H^1=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{R})=\mathbb{R}$, $H^2=0$, the same as for a circle; for $\mathbb{RP}^2$, $H^0=\mathbb{R}$ and $H^1=H^2=0$, the same as for a point. (The vanishing of $H^2$ in both cases also matches non-orientability.) If $2c=\partial b$ and $\omega$ is closed, then $2\int_c\omega=\int_{\partial b}\omega=\int_bd\omega=0$. Kedlaya's notes give an algebraic instance: on an Enriques surface the canonical bundle defines a nontrivial $2$-torsion class in $H^2$, and like every torsion class it maps to zero in de Rham cohomology with real or complex coefficients.

blocks.title: Integral classes and quantised fluxes
blocks.body: The image of $H^k(M;\mathbb{Z})\to H^k(M;\mathbb{R})\cong H^k_{dR}(M)$ is called the lattice of integral classes. Show that a class is integral (in this image) exactly when all its periods over integral cycles are integers, assuming $H_k(M)$ finitely generated, and explain how this matches flux quantisation for a $2$-form $F$ with $\int_{S^2}F\in\mathbb{Z}$.
blocks.solution: With $H_k(M)\cong\mathbb{Z}^b\oplus T$, the universal coefficient theorem identifies the free part of $H^k(M;\mathbb{Z})$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^b,\mathbb{Z})$, and its image in $\operatorname{Hom}(H_k(M),\mathbb{R})$ consists of the homomorphisms taking integer values on $\mathbb{Z}^b$ (torsion classes map to zero). Under $I$, this is the condition $\int_z\omega\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all integral cycles $z$. On $M=\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, $H_2=\mathbb{Z}$ generated by the unit sphere, so a closed $2$-form is integral exactly when its flux through $S^2$ is an integer. In the normalisation of Bhardwaj et al. ('t Hooft lines carry magnetic charge $q$ with $\int_{S^2}F=q\in\mathbb{Z}$), quantisation of magnetic flux is precisely the statement that $[F]$ is an integral class. Lim's discussion of the exponential sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{E}^\times\to0$ explains where integrality comes from for line bundles: smooth complex line bundles are classified by $H^2(X;\mathbb{Z})$, and the first Chern form represents the image of this integral class.

blocks.body:
- De Rham cohomology is real cohomology. It loses all torsion of $H^*(M;\mathbb{Z})$: the Klein bottle has $H^1_{dR}=\mathbb{R}$, like a circle, and $\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ has the de Rham cohomology of a point. Statements about integral classes (Chern classes in $H^2(M;\mathbb{Z})$, flux quantisation) need extra input beyond forms.
- Singular simplices are only continuous, and a form cannot be integrated over a continuous simplex. The smoothing theorem is a genuine step of the proof, not a formality.
- The isomorphism goes to cohomology, not homology: de Rham classes are functionals on cycles. On a compact oriented manifold Poincaré duality identifies $H^k$ with $H^{n-k}$, which is why papers sometimes blur the two, but on non-compact manifolds they differ.
- Homotopy invariance of de Rham cohomology does not require de Rham's theorem (it was proved directly above), but topological invariance under homeomorphisms that are not smooth does.

1. Show directly from the definitions that $I:H^0(M)\to H^0(M;\mathbb{R})$ is an isomorphism for every $M$.
2. Using $H_1(\Sigma_g)=\mathbb{Z}^{2g}$ for the closed orientable surface of genus $g$, compute $H^*_{dR}(\Sigma_g)$, and check Poincaré duality and $\chi=2-2g$.
3. Let $\omega$ be a closed $1$-form on $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{p,q\}$ with $\int_{\gamma_p}\omega=\int_{\gamma_q}\omega=0$. Show that $\omega$ is exact, and write $\omega_p-\omega_q$ plus an exact form for a form with periods $(2\pi,-2\pi)$.
4. For the nonorientable surface $N_k$ with $H_1(N_k)=\mathbb{Z}^{k-1}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2=0$, compute $H^*_{dR}(N_k)$.
5. Show that the class of the area form of $S^2$ divided by $4\pi$ is integral, and that the class of $\Phi/(4\pi)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$ (with $\Phi$ from the flux example) is a generator of the integral lattice.

blocks.title: Betti numbers and what they count
blocks.body:
For a manifold with finite-dimensional cohomology the Betti numbers $b_k=\dim H^k(M)$ are, by de Rham's theorem, the ranks of the integral homology groups of [[homology]], so the two pages' Betti numbers agree. Applied papers read them as counts of features. Su–Tong–Wei, who work with domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (compact $3$-manifolds with boundary carved out of a grid), interpret $b_0$ as the number of connected components, $b_1$ as the number of tunnels (independent loops that cannot be filled in) and $b_2$ as the number of cavities (enclosed voids). López Neumann gives the matching reading for open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$: $H^0$ counts components, $H^1$ measures curl-free fields that are not gradients (for example on $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus a line), $H^2$ measures divergence-free fields that are not curls (for example on $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus a point), and in general the failure reflects holes of the domain.

For a region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$ these numbers are computed from forms: $b_1$ is the number of independent curl-free fields modulo gradients, and $b_2$ the number of independent divergence-free fields modulo curls.

blocks.title: Solid torus, spherical shell and their complements
blocks.body: Compute the Betti numbers of (a) an open solid torus $D$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, (b) the open spherical shell $\{1< |x|< 2\}$, (c) $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus a closed solid torus, and identify representing forms or fields.
blocks.solution:
(a) $D$ deformation retracts onto its core circle, so $b=(1,1,0,0)$. A representative of $H^1$ is the angle form $(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/(x^2+y^2)$ around the axis through the hole (with the torus placed around the $z$-axis), restricted to $D$: one tunnel.

(b) The shell retracts onto $S^2$: $b=(1,0,1,0)$. The field $x/|x|^3$, as the $2$-form $\Phi$, represents $H^2$: one cavity.

(c) Let $W$ be the complement of a closed solid torus $\bar D$ and $D'$ a slightly larger open solid torus, so that $\mathbb{R}^3=W\cup D'$ and $W\cap D'$ is a thickened torus surface, homotopy equivalent to $T^2$. Since $H^k(\mathbb{R}^3)=0$ for $k\ge1$, the Mayer–Vietoris sequence breaks into isomorphisms $H^k(W)\oplus H^k(D')\cong H^k(T^2)$ for $k=1,2$ (and $H^3(W)=0$). With $H^1(D')=\mathbb{R}$, $H^2(D')=0$ and $b(T^2)=(1,2,1)$, this gives $b_1(W)=1$ and $b_2(W)=1$, so $b(W)=(1,1,1,0)$. The $H^1$ class is represented by the field of a steady current along the core circle of the torus (it circulates around the tube; its integral around a small meridian loop is nonzero), and the $H^2$ class by the flux of a field with a point source inside $\bar D$ through the boundary torus.

blocks.body:
1. Compute the Betti numbers of $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus two disjoint closed balls, and of $\mathbb{R}^3$ minus two disjoint lines.
2. A compact domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$ is a solid handlebody of genus $g$ (a thickened graph with $g$ independent loops). Show $b=(1,g,0,0)$.
3. Show that for a compact connected domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$ with smooth boundary, $\chi(\Omega)=1-b_1+b_2$, and compute it for the solid torus and the shell.

blocks.title: Sheaves and Čech cohomology
blocks.body:
Complex geometry papers such as Lim's survey use de Rham cohomology through sheaf theory (see [[sheaves]] and [[sheaf-cohomology]]). The dictionary is short.

Let $\underline{\mathbb{R}}$ be the sheaf of locally constant real functions and $\mathcal{E}^k$ the sheaf $U\mapsto\Omega^k(U)$. The sequence of sheaves
$$0\to\underline{\mathbb{R}}\to\mathcal{E}^0\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{E}^1\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{E}^2\to\cdots$$
is exact, because exactness of sheaves is a local condition and locally it is the Poincaré lemma on balls (plus $H^0$ of a ball being the constants). So it is a resolution of $\underline{\mathbb{R}}$. Each $\mathcal{E}^k$ is fine (it admits partitions of unity), and fine sheaves on paracompact spaces have no higher cohomology. A resolution by such acyclic sheaves computes sheaf cohomology from global sections, so
$$H^k(M;\underline{\mathbb{R}})\cong H^k\big(\Omega^*(M),d\big)=H^k_{dR}(M).$$
The same mechanism, with the sheaf of smooth singular cochains, gives de Rham's theorem in Lim's Theorem 2.2; with the holomorphic forms $\Omega^p$ resolved by smooth $(p,q)$-forms it gives Dolbeault's theorem (Lim, Theorem 2.3), which is outside this page.

Čech side. For an open cover $\mathfrak{U}=\{U_\alpha\}$, a Čech $p$-cochain with real coefficients assigns a real number $c_{\alpha_0\cdots\alpha_p}$ to each ordered $(p+1)$-tuple with $U_{\alpha_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{\alpha_p}\ne\varnothing$, alternating in the indices, with coboundary $(\delta c)_{\alpha_0\cdots\alpha_{p+1}}=\sum_i(-1)^ic_{\alpha_0\cdots\widehat{\alpha_i}\cdots\alpha_{p+1}}$. For a good cover this is the simplicial cochain complex of the nerve (the simplicial complex with a vertex for each $U_\alpha$ and a $p$-simplex for each nonempty $(p+1)$-fold intersection). Bott–Tu (Chapter II, §8) prove, with the Čech–de Rham double complex and the Mayer–Vietoris principle for many open sets, that for a good cover $H^*_{dR}(M)\cong\check H^*(\mathfrak{U};\mathbb{R})$; Guillemin–Haine (§5.8) sketch the same argument for manifolds of finite topology. We state this without proof.

blocks.title: The circle from the nerve of a three-arc cover
blocks.body: Cover $S^1$ by three open arcs $U_0,U_1,U_2$, each slightly more than a third of the circle, so that consecutive arcs overlap in an arc and the triple intersection is empty. Compute the Čech cohomology of this cover.
blocks.solution: Each $U_i$ and each nonempty $U_i\cap U_j$ is an arc, so the cover is good. The nerve has $3$ vertices and the $3$ edges $\{0,1\},\{0,2\},\{1,2\}$, and no triangle: it is the hollow triangle of [[homology]]. Čech $0$-cochains are $\mathbb{R}^3$, $1$-cochains $\mathbb{R}^3$, and $\delta:C^0\to C^1$, $(\delta c)_{ij}=c_j-c_i$, is the transpose of the boundary matrix $\partial_1$ of the hollow triangle, of rank $2$. So $\check H^0=\ker\delta=\mathbb{R}$ (constant cochains) and $\check H^1=\mathbb{R}^3/\operatorname{im}\delta=\mathbb{R}$, in agreement with $H^*_{dR}(S^1)$.

2. Explain why the cover of $S^1$ by two arcs is not good, and show that the Čech complex of its nerve (one edge between two vertices) gives $\check H^1=0$: goodness of the cover is needed.

blocks.title: Harmonic forms and the Hodge decomposition
blocks.body:
A Riemannian metric picks out a best representative in each cohomology class. Full proofs belong to [[hodge-theory]]; here are the definitions and statements in the form papers use them, following Su–Tong–Wei's preliminaries.

Let $M$ be an oriented Riemannian $m$-manifold with volume form $\mu$. The metric gives an inner product $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$ on $k$-forms at each point (the one for which $dx_I$, $|I|=k$, is orthonormal when $dx_1,\dots,dx_m$ is). The Hodge star $\star:\Omega^k\to\Omega^{m-k}$ is defined by
$$\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\,\mu,$$
and on a compact $M$ the $L^2$ inner product is $(\alpha,\beta)=\int_M\alpha\wedge\star\beta$. In $\mathbb{R}^m$ with the Euclidean metric, $\star dx_I=\pm dx_{I^c}$ with the sign making $dx_I\wedge\star dx_I=\mu$; for instance in $\mathbb{R}^3$, $\star dx=dy\wedge dz$, $\star dy=dz\wedge dx$, $\star dz=dx\wedge dy$, and $\star\star=(-1)^{k(m-k)}$ on $k$-forms. The codifferential on $k$-forms is
$$\delta=(-1)^{m(k-1)+1}\star d\star:\Omega^k\to\Omega^{k-1},$$
the formal adjoint of $d$: $(d\alpha,\beta)=(\alpha,\delta\beta)$ on a closed manifold. The Hodge Laplacian is $\Delta=d\delta+\delta d$, and $\omega$ is harmonic if $\Delta\omega=0$. On a closed manifold, $(\Delta\omega,\omega)=\|d\omega\|^2+\|\delta\omega\|^2$, so harmonic means $d\omega=0$ and $\delta\omega=0$ (Su–Tong–Wei, Eq. 7). For functions on $\mathbb{R}^m$, $\Delta f=-\sum_i\partial_i^2f$, the analyst's Laplacian with the opposite sign.

blocks.title: Hodge theorem (statement)
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be a closed (compact, no boundary) oriented Riemannian manifold and $\mathcal{H}^k$ the space of harmonic $k$-forms. Then
$$\Omega^k(M)=d\Omega^{k-1}(M)\oplus\delta\Omega^{k+1}(M)\oplus\mathcal{H}^k,$$
an $L^2$-orthogonal direct sum, and the map $\mathcal{H}^k\to H^k(M)$, $\omega\mapsto[\omega]$, is an isomorphism. So every de Rham class contains exactly one harmonic form, $\dim\mathcal{H}^k=b_k$, and the harmonic representative is the unique form of least $L^2$ norm in its class. The proof of the decomposition (elliptic regularity) is on [[hodge-theory]]; Lim's survey proves it as the first step towards the Kodaira embedding theorem. The norm statement follows from the decomposition, as shown next.

blocks.title: Proof that harmonic representatives minimise the norm
blocks.body: Assume the decomposition. A closed form $\omega$ is orthogonal to $\delta\Omega^{k+1}$, since $(\omega,\delta\beta)=(d\omega,\beta)=0$; so $\omega=d\alpha+h$ with $h$ harmonic, and $[\omega]=[h]$. If $h,h'$ are harmonic and cohomologous, $h-h'=d\alpha$ is both harmonic and exact, hence orthogonal to itself: $(d\alpha,d\alpha)=(\alpha,\delta(h-h'))=0$. For minimality, $\|h+d\alpha\|^2=\|h\|^2+2(h,d\alpha)+\|d\alpha\|^2=\|h\|^2+\|d\alpha\|^2$, because $(h,d\alpha)=(\delta h,\alpha)=0$.

blocks.title: Harmonic representatives

items.label: Best representative
items.body: Each class on a compact oriented Riemannian manifold contains exactly one harmonic form, and it is the one of least $L^2$ norm (least energy). A class, an abstract coset, becomes a concrete form once a metric is chosen.

items.label: Orthogonal splitting
items.body: Su–Tong–Wei use the Hodge decomposition itself: any form splits uniquely and orthogonally into exact, coexact and harmonic parts, the vector-calculus version being gradient plus curl plus a harmonic field, and the harmonic part is the topological signal.

items.label: Kernel of a matrix
items.body: After discretisation (their §3) harmonic forms are null vectors of a sparse symmetric matrix, the discrete Hodge Laplacian, and Betti numbers are nullities; persistence tracks these nullities along a filtration.

items.label: Gateway to complex geometry
items.body: Lim's survey treats the isomorphism between harmonic forms and de Rham cohomology as the analytic input from which, on Kähler manifolds, the Hodge decomposition and eventually the Kodaira embedding theorem are derived.

blocks.title: Harmonic representatives on the circle and the flat torus
blocks.body: (a) On $S^1$ with the metric $d\theta^2$, find the harmonic representative of the class of $g(\theta)\,d\theta$. (b) On the flat torus $T^n=\mathbb{R}^n/2\pi\mathbb{Z}^n$, show that the forms with constant coefficients in $d\theta_I$ are harmonic.
blocks.solution:
(a) Here $m=1$, $\star d\theta=1$ and $\star1=d\theta$. For a $1$-form, $\delta(g\,d\theta)=(-1)^{1\cdot0+1}\star d\star(g\,d\theta)=-\star dg=-g'$, and on functions $\delta=0$. So $\Delta(g\,d\theta)=d\delta(g\,d\theta)=-g''\,d\theta$, and $g\,d\theta$ is harmonic exactly when $g$ is constant ($g''=0$ and periodic). The class of $g\,d\theta$ is determined by $\int g$, so its harmonic representative is $\bar g\,d\theta$ with $\bar g=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}g$, and $g\,d\theta=\bar g\,d\theta+df$ with $f=\int_0^\theta(g-\bar g)$, as in the first example. The minimality is the inequality $\int_0^{2\pi}g^2\ge2\pi\bar g^2$, which is Cauchy–Schwarz.

(b) In flat coordinates the metric is Euclidean, $\star$ sends $d\theta_I$ to $\pm d\theta_{I^c}$ with constant coefficients, and $d$ of a constant-coefficient form is zero. So $d\omega=0$ and $\delta\omega=\pm\star d\star\omega=0$. There are $\binom nk$ independent such $k$-forms, which is $b_k(T^n)$, so by the Hodge theorem they are all the harmonic forms, and they represent the classes found by Künneth.

blocks.title: Manifolds with boundary: absolute and relative cohomology
blocks.body:
Applied papers work on compact domains with boundary, and there the harmonic fields $\{\omega:d\omega=0,\ \delta\omega=0\}$ form an infinite-dimensional space (on a disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$, for instance, $u\,dx-v\,dy$ is closed and coclosed for every holomorphic function $u+iv$, by the Cauchy–Riemann equations). Su–Tong–Wei explain how boundary conditions cut it down. Integration by parts acquires a boundary term, $(d\omega,\eta)=(\omega,\delta\eta)+\int_{\partial M}\omega\wedge\star\eta$, and they introduce two subspaces:
- normal (Dirichlet) forms $\Omega^k_n=\{\omega:\ \omega|_{\partial M}=0\}$, meaning the pullback of $\omega$ to $\partial M$ vanishes;
- tangential (Neumann) forms $\Omega^k_t=\{\omega:\ \star\omega|_{\partial M}=0\}$.

$d$ preserves the normal condition and $\delta$ the tangential one, and $\star$ exchanges them. The normal forms form a subcomplex whose cohomology is the relative de Rham cohomology $H^k(M,\partial M)$, and the space $\mathcal{H}^k_n$ of harmonic fields with normal boundary condition is isomorphic to it, with dimension $b_{m-k}$; the harmonic fields with tangential boundary condition $\mathcal{H}^k_t$ are isomorphic to the absolute cohomology $H^k(M)$, of dimension $b_k$. They also quote the Hodge–Morrey decomposition $\Omega^k=d\Omega^{k-1}_n\oplus\delta\Omega^{k+1}_t\oplus\mathcal{H}^k$ and its refinement, the Hodge–Morrey–Friedrichs decomposition. (In the paragraph after their Remark 2 the definition of $\mathcal{H}^k_t$ is misprinted as $\mathcal{H}^k_t\cap\Omega^k_t$; the intended space is the harmonic fields lying in $\Omega^k_t$, as in the normal case.) Proofs are not covered here; see the references in Su–Tong–Wei, §2.1.

blocks.title: The interval
blocks.body: For $M=[0,1]$ compute the absolute cohomology $H^*(M)$, the relative cohomology $H^*(M,\partial M)$ from the complex of normal forms, and check the dimensions $b_k$ and $b_{m-k}$.
blocks.solution: Absolute: $H^0=\mathbb{R}$ (constants) and every $f\,dx$ is exact, so $H^1=0$; $b=(1,0)$. Relative: the normal $0$-forms are the functions vanishing at $0$ and $1$; the pullback of a $1$-form to the boundary points is automatically $0$, so all $1$-forms are normal. Closed normal $0$-forms are constants vanishing at the ends, so $H^0(M,\partial M)=0$. A $1$-form $f\,dx$ is $dg$ with $g(0)=g(1)=0$ if and only if $\int_0^1f=0$ (take $g(x)=\int_0^xf$), so $H^1(M,\partial M)\cong\mathbb{R}$ via $\int_0^1$. The dimensions are $(0,1)=(b_{1-0},b_{1-1})$, as stated. Harmonic fields: on $[0,1]$ they are the constant functions and the constant multiples of $dx$. The normal condition kills the constant functions and keeps $dx$, so $\mathcal{H}^*_n$ has dimensions $(0,1)$; the tangential condition asks that $\star\omega$ pull back to zero at the endpoints, which is automatic for functions ($\star1=dx$) and forces $c=0$ for $c\,dx$ ($\star(c\,dx)=c$), so $\mathcal{H}^*_t$ has dimensions $(1,0)$, matching $H^*(M)$.

blocks.title: Codifferential and Hodge star signs
blocks.body: The sign in front of $\star d\star$ varies with how it is written; in Riemannian signature the common versions agree. Check against adjointness, $(d\alpha,\beta)=(\alpha,\delta\beta)$, which fixes $\delta$ uniquely.

rows.text: $\delta=(-1)^{m(k-1)+1}\star d\star$ on $k$-forms of an $m$-manifold, $\Delta=d\delta+\delta d$.

Since $m(k-1)$ and $m(k+1)$ differ by $2m$, the same operator is $(-1)^{m(k+1)+1}\star d\star$; and since $\star\star=(-1)^{j(m-j)}$ on $j$-forms in Riemannian signature, it is also $(-1)^k\star^{-1}d\star$. All three are one operator.

In general signature the definition of $\delta$ carries an extra factor $s$, the sign (parity) of the signature of the metric, and $\star\star=s(-1)^{k(m-k)}$; in Lorentzian physics papers this changes signs relative to the Riemannian formulas.
$\Delta=d\delta+\delta d$ is a nonnegative operator; on functions in $\mathbb{R}^m$ it is $-\sum\partial_i^2$, the negative of the usual analyst's Laplacian.

blocks.title: Discrete de Rham complexes
blocks.body:
Numerical analysts and topological data analysts replace forms by cochains on a mesh, and the de Rham complex by the simplicial cochain complex. The bridge is integration. For a simplicial (or cubical) complex $K$ triangulating a domain, the de Rham map $\mathcal{R}:\Omega^k\to C^k(K;\mathbb{R})$ records the integrals of a $k$-form over the oriented $k$-cells, $(\mathcal{R}\omega)(\sigma)=\int_\sigma\omega$; Su–Tong–Wei store a discrete $k$-form as exactly this vector of integrals. The discrete exterior derivative $D_k:C^k\to C^{k+1}$ is the transpose of the boundary matrix $\partial_{k+1}$ of [[homology]], so $D_{k+1}D_k=0$ because $\partial\partial=0$, and Stokes' theorem on each cell is the commuting relation
$$D_k\,\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}\,d,\qquad\text{since}\quad(\mathcal{R}d\omega)(\tau)=\int_\tau d\omega=\int_{\partial\tau}\omega=(\mathcal{R}\omega)(\partial\tau).$$
Guzmán–Hirani–Liu–Potu use this together with the Whitney map $W$ from cochains to piecewise polynomial forms, which satisfies $dW=WD$ and $\mathcal{R}W=\mathrm{id}$ (they refer to Whitney's book for both), so cochains can be turned back into genuine forms without changing the cohomology. Their discrete Poincaré operators are built from cone operators on chains: a map $\mathrm{Co}$ raising dimension by one with
$$\mathrm{Co}(\partial\sigma)+\partial\,\mathrm{Co}(\sigma)=\sigma\ (\dim\sigma\ge1),\qquad\partial\,\mathrm{Co}(v)=v-a\ \ (\text{vertices}),$$
for a fixed vertex $a$; on a complex that is star-shaped with respect to $a$, $\mathrm{Co}[v_0,\dots,v_k]=[a,v_0,\dots,v_k]$ (zero if $a$ is already a vertex of the simplex). The dual operator $P$ on cochains, $(P\alpha)(\sigma)=\alpha(\mathrm{Co}\,\sigma)$, satisfies $DP+PD=\mathrm{id}$ on cochains of positive degree, the discrete counterpart of $dK+Kd=\mathrm{id}$.

Hodge theory becomes linear algebra. Su–Tong–Wei use diagonal discrete Hodge stars $S_k$ (ratios of dual to primal cell volumes) and the discrete Laplacian $L_k=D_k^{\mathsf T}S_{k+1}D_k+S_kD_{k-1}S_{k-1}^{-1}D_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}S_k$; replacing all stars by identities gives $L^B_k=D_k^{\mathsf T}D_k+D_{k-1}D_{k-1}^{\mathsf T}$, with the same kernel dimensions. In every version, $\dim\ker L_k=b_k$ of the complex: the discrete Hodge theorem, which in finite dimensions is just the orthogonal decomposition $C^k=\operatorname{im}D_{k-1}\oplus\operatorname{im}D_k^{\mathsf T}\oplus\ker L_k$.

blocks.title: Betti numbers as kernels of Laplacian matrices
blocks.body: Compute $\ker L^B_k$ for the hollow triangle (three vertices, three edges) and for the boundary of a tetrahedron, and compare with the Betti numbers from [[homology]].
blocks.solution:
Hollow triangle, edges ordered $[0,1],[0,2],[1,2]$: $D_0=\partial_1^{\mathsf T}$ has rows $(-1,1,0)$, $(-1,0,1)$, $(0,-1,1)$. Then $L^B_0=D_0^{\mathsf T}D_0$ is the graph Laplacian $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&-1\\-1&2&-1\\-1&-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, with kernel the constants: $\dim=1=b_0$. There are no $2$-cells, so $L^B_1=D_0D_0^{\mathsf T}$, a $3\times3$ matrix of rank $2$, with kernel spanned by $(1,-1,1)$, the cochain $[0,1]-[0,2]+[1,2]$ dual to the cycle $z$ of [[homology]]: $\dim=1=b_1$.

Tetrahedron boundary ($4$ vertices, $6$ edges, $4$ triangles): $\operatorname{rank}D_0=3$ and $\operatorname{rank}D_1=3$, so $\dim\ker L^B_0=4-3=1$, $\dim\ker L^B_1=6-3-3=0$, $\dim\ker L^B_2=4-3=1$. These are $b=(1,0,1)$ of the sphere. In general $\dim\ker L_k=\dim C^k-\operatorname{rank}D_k-\operatorname{rank}D_{k-1}$, which is $\dim\ker D_k-\dim\operatorname{im}D_{k-1}$.

blocks.title: A discrete Poincaré operator on a triangle
blocks.body: On the filled triangle with vertices $0,1,2$ and cone vertex $a=0$, write down $\mathrm{Co}$, check the cone identity, and use $P$ to find a $0$-cochain $\beta$ with $D\beta=\alpha$ for the closed $1$-cochain $\alpha$ with values $\alpha[0,1]=2$, $\alpha[0,2]=5$, $\alpha[1,2]=3$.
blocks.solution:
$\mathrm{Co}[0]=0$, $\mathrm{Co}[1]=[0,1]$, $\mathrm{Co}[2]=[0,2]$, $\mathrm{Co}[1,2]=[0,1,2]$, and $\mathrm{Co}[0,1]=\mathrm{Co}[0,2]=0$ (degenerate). Check on $[1,2]$: $\partial\mathrm{Co}[1,2]=[1,2]-[0,2]+[0,1]$ and $\mathrm{Co}\,\partial[1,2]=\mathrm{Co}([2]-[1])=[0,2]-[0,1]$, with sum $[1,2]$. On $[0,1]$: $\mathrm{Co}\,\partial[0,1]=\mathrm{Co}([1]-[0])=[0,1]$. On vertices, $\partial\mathrm{Co}[v]=v-[0]$.

$\alpha$ is closed: $(D\alpha)[0,1,2]=\alpha(\partial[0,1,2])=\alpha[1,2]-\alpha[0,2]+\alpha[0,1]=3-5+2=0$. Put $\beta=P\alpha$: $\beta[0]=\alpha(0)=0$, $\beta[1]=\alpha[0,1]=2$, $\beta[2]=\alpha[0,2]=5$. Then $D\beta[0,1]=\beta[1]-\beta[0]=2$, $D\beta[0,2]=5$, $D\beta[1,2]=3$: $D\beta=\alpha$. This is the discrete version of integrating a closed $1$-form along rays from the cone point.

blocks.title: Curvature and characteristic classes
blocks.body:
The most frequent source of de Rham classes in geometry and physics is curvature. The full theory is on [[curvature-forms]] (with [[vector-bundles]]); what papers assume from this page is the following mechanism. A connection on a complex vector bundle $E$ of rank $r$ is described, over an open set where $E$ has a frame, by an $r\times r$ matrix $\theta$ of $1$-forms; its curvature is the matrix of $2$-forms $\Theta=d\theta+\theta\wedge\theta$ (Lim, Proposition 2.10, writes $\Theta=d\theta+\theta^2$; Notman–Sanabani write $F=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega$). Under a change of frame $\Theta$ is conjugated, so invariant polynomials of $\Theta$, such as $\operatorname{tr}\Theta^k$ or the coefficients of $\det(I+t\Theta)$, are globally defined forms. Two facts make them cohomology classes:
1. They are closed. This follows from the Bianchi identity $d\Theta=\Theta\wedge\theta-\theta\wedge\Theta$ (Lim, Proposition 2.11, $d\Theta=[\Theta,\theta]$): for instance $d\operatorname{tr}\Theta^k=k\operatorname{tr}(d\Theta\wedge\Theta^{k-1})=k\operatorname{tr}([\Theta,\theta]\Theta^{k-1})=0$, a trace of a graded commutator.
2. Their classes do not depend on the connection (Notman–Sanabani, Corollary 2.90; Lim states it as Proposition 2.16 and only indicates the interpolation argument). Wikipedia's proof is by homotopy invariance: join two connections by the path $\theta_t=(1-t)\theta_0+t\theta_1$, regard it as one connection on $E\times\mathbb{R}\to M\times\mathbb{R}$, and pull back along the inclusions at $t=0$ and $t=1$, which are homotopic.

For a line bundle ($r=1$) everything is scalar and can be checked by hand, as in the next example. The resulting classes are the Chern classes; their normalisations differ between sources.

blocks.title: Line bundles: closed curvature, connection-independent class
blocks.body: For a complex line bundle, a connection is given by local $1$-forms $\theta_\alpha$ on a cover, with $\theta_\beta=\theta_\alpha+g_{\alpha\beta}^{-1}dg_{\alpha\beta}$ for the transition functions $g_{\alpha\beta}$ (Lim's frame-change rule for $r=1$). Show that the curvature $\Theta=d\theta_\alpha$ is a well-defined closed $2$-form, and that changing the connection changes $\Theta$ by an exact form.
blocks.solution: For $r=1$, $\theta\wedge\theta=0$, so $\Theta=d\theta_\alpha$ locally. On overlaps $d\theta_\beta-d\theta_\alpha=d(g^{-1}dg)=d(d\log g)=0$ locally (where a branch of $\log g$ exists; in general $d(g^{-1}dg)=-g^{-2}dg\wedge dg=0$), so the local forms agree and $\Theta$ is global. It is closed, being locally exact. For a second connection $\theta'_\alpha$, the differences $a=\theta'_\alpha-\theta_\alpha$ agree on overlaps (the $g^{-1}dg$ terms cancel), so $a$ is a global $1$-form and $\Theta'-\Theta=da$ is exact. Hence $[\Theta]\in H^2(M;\mathbb{C})$ depends only on the bundle. With Lim's normalisation, $c_1(L)=\big[\tfrac{\sqrt{-1}}{2\pi}\Theta\big]$; it is the image of an integral class (the exponential sequence), so its integral over every closed oriented surface is an integer. Note that $\Theta$ itself is only locally exact: $[\Theta]$ is the obstruction to finding one global $\theta$.

blocks.title: Normalising Chern classes and equivariant differentials
blocks.body: These conventions change signs and factors of $2\pi$ and $i$ in formulas that papers quote without comment.

rows.text: $c(E)=\det\big(I+\tfrac{\sqrt{-1}}{2\pi}\Theta\big)$, the $k$-th Chern form being its degree-$2k$ part; so $c_1=\tfrac{\sqrt{-1}}{2\pi}\operatorname{tr}\Theta$.

$c_k=\varepsilon_k(F)/(2\pi i)^k$ (their Example 2.93), where $\det(I+tA)=\sum_kt^k\varepsilon_k(A)$ (Definition 2.91) and $F=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega$ as in Lim. Since $1/(2\pi i)=-i/(2\pi)$, this differs from Lim's $c_k$ by $(-1)^k$ for the same curvature matrix, so compare on a known example before mixing formulas: for the line bundle of the first exercise below, Lim's formula gives $\int_{S^2}c_1=-1$ and the formula as printed in Notman–Sanabani gives $+1$.
Defines Chern classes through the characteristic polynomial in a variable $t$ and notes that its source uses $t^{-1}$ in place of $t$; the two choices reorder the coefficients.

Cartan differential $d_G=1\otimes d-\sum_i\xi^i\otimes\iota_{\xi_i}$, equivalently $(d_G\alpha)(\xi)=d(\alpha(\xi))-\iota_{\xi}\alpha(\xi)$. Meinrenken defines the generating vector field of $\xi\in\mathfrak g$ using $\exp(-t\xi)$, and puts a factor $2\pi$ inside his equivariant Euler form; signs in localisation formulas depend on both choices.

Tate twist $\mathbb{Q}(k)=(2\pi i)^k\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{C}$; a de Rham class of degree $2k$ is compared with Betti classes after dividing periods by $(2\pi i)^k$, which is what makes algebraic cycle classes rational on both sides.

blocks.title: Equivariant cohomology: the Cartan model
blocks.body:
When a compact Lie group $G$ acts on $M$ (see [[lie-groups]] and [[lie-algebras]]), each $\xi\in\mathfrak g$ gives a vector field $\xi_M$ on $M$. Notman–Sanabani and Meinrenken define the Cartan complex
$$\Omega_G(M)=\big(S(\mathfrak g^*)\otimes\Omega(M)\big)^G,$$
the $G$-invariant polynomial maps $\alpha:\mathfrak g\to\Omega(M)$, graded so that elements of $\mathfrak g^*$ have degree $2$, with differential
$$(d_G\alpha)(\xi)=d\big(\alpha(\xi)\big)-\iota_{\xi_M}\alpha(\xi).$$
Its cohomology is the equivariant cohomology $H_G(M)$; Cartan's theorem identifies it with the cohomology of the Borel construction $(M\times EG)/G$ (Notman–Sanabani, Theorem 3.10; Meinrenken, Theorem 6.1, for compact connected $G$) and with the Weil model (Meinrenken, Theorem 5.3). We do not prove this. What one can see directly is why the invariance condition is needed.

blocks.title: The Cartan differential squares to zero on invariant forms
blocks.body: For $\alpha\in S(\mathfrak g^*)\otimes\Omega(M)$, $(d_G^2\alpha)(\xi)=-L_{\xi_M}\big(\alpha(\xi)\big)$. In particular $d_G^2=0$ on the $G$-invariant subcomplex.

Fix $\xi$ and write $\iota=\iota_{\xi_M}$, a fixed vector field, so $d_G$ acts as $d-\iota$ on the form $\alpha(\xi)$. Then $(d-\iota)^2=d^2-(d\iota+\iota d)+\iota^2=-L_{\xi_M}$ by Cartan's formula, since $d^2=0$ and $\iota^2=0$. Invariance under the connected group $G$ implies infinitesimal invariance, $L_{\xi_M}\alpha(\xi)=0$ (the $G$-action on $\Omega_G$ combines the action on forms with the coadjoint action on polynomials, and evaluated at $\xi$ the latter contributes nothing for the derivative in the direction $\xi$ itself). Notman–Sanabani's Proposition 3.6 states $d_G^2=0$; the computation above shows that the invariance restriction is essential.

blocks.title: The rotating sphere: an equivariantly closed form and localisation
blocks.body: Let $S^1$ rotate $S^2$ about the $z$-axis, with generating field $X=\partial_\varphi$ (angle $\varphi$ around the axis), and use $u$ for the degree-$2$ generator of $S(\mathfrak g^*)$, so $d_X=d-u\,\iota_X$. Let $\mu=d\varphi\wedge dz$, the area form in cylindrical coordinates $(\varphi,z)$. Show that $\mu+u\,z$ is equivariantly closed, and compute $\int_{S^2}e^{tz}\mu$ to see the shape of the Duistermaat–Heckman formula.
blocks.solution:
$\mu=d\varphi\wedge dz$ is the area form with the outward orientation (at $(1,0,0)$, the frame (normal, $\partial_\varphi$, $\partial_z$) is the standard basis), and by Archimedes' observation its integral is $2\pi\cdot2=4\pi$. Since $\iota_X(d\varphi\wedge dz)=dz$,
$$d_X(\mu+uz)=d\mu+u\,dz-u\,\iota_X\mu-u^2\iota_Xz=0+u\,dz-u\,dz-0=0 .$$
So $\mu+uz$ is equivariantly closed: the height $z$ is a Hamiltonian (moment map) for the rotation. Now
$$\int_{S^2}e^{tz}\mu=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{-1}^1e^{tz}\,dz\,d\varphi=\frac{2\pi}{t}\big(e^{t}-e^{-t}\big)=\frac{2\pi\,e^{t\cdot1}}{t}+\frac{2\pi\,e^{t\cdot(-1)}}{-t}.$$
The right side is a sum over the two fixed points of the rotation, the poles $z=\pm1$, of $e^{t\,z(p)}$ divided by a weight $\pm t/2\pi$ of the action at $p$. This is exactly the shape of the Duistermaat–Heckman theorem quoted by Notman–Sanabani (Theorem 3.30), $\int_M\frac{\omega^n}{n!}e^{\mu(X)}=\sum_{p}\frac{e^{\mu(p)(X)}}{e^T(\nu_p,X)}$; the factor $2\pi$ and the signs belong to the normalisation of the equivariant Euler class, which Meinrenken builds into his Euler form. The integral of an equivariantly closed form is determined by the fixed points, and the computation is exact, not an approximation.

blocks.title: Equivariant integration, the point and fixed points
blocks.body:
Papers that use the Cartan model do three things with it besides writing down equivariantly closed forms: they compute the equivariant cohomology of a point, they restrict classes to fixed points, and they integrate. Each is a short consequence of the definitions of the previous section. We keep its conventions, $d_G=d-\iota$ with elements of $\mathfrak g^*$ in degree $2$; Libine's notes (Definitions 16 and 19) use the same sign and grading.

The point. For $M=\mathrm{pt}$ the only forms are constants in degree $0$, and $d$ and every $\iota_{\xi_M}$ vanish. So $\Omega_G(\mathrm{pt})=S(\mathfrak g^*)^G$ with zero differential, and
$$H_G(\mathrm{pt})=S(\mathfrak g^*)^G,$$
as in Notman–Sanabani, Example 3.13, and Libine, §5.4. For a torus $T$ of rank $r$ the coadjoint action is trivial, so $H_T(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb{R}[u_1,\dots,u_r]$ with $\deg u_j=2$; this is the real form of the topological answer $H^*(BT;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\dots,x_r]$ in Notman–Sanabani's Example 2.77. For the circle we write $u$ for the generator, as before.

Module structure. If $q\in S(\mathfrak g^*)^G$ and $\alpha\in\Omega_G(M)$, then $q\alpha\in\Omega_G(M)$ and $d_G(q\alpha)=q\,d_G\alpha$, because $d$ and $\iota$ act only on the form factor. Hence cocycles and coboundaries are stable under multiplication by $S(\mathfrak g^*)^G$, and $H_G(M)$ is a module over $H_G(\mathrm{pt})$. This is the Cartan-model form of the module structure in Notman–Sanabani, Theorem 2.78, and in Meinrenken, §2, where it comes from the map $M\to\mathrm{pt}$.

Restriction to a fixed point. If $p\in M$ is fixed by $G$, every generating field vanishes at $p$. The inclusion $i_p:\mathrm{pt}\to M$ kills forms of positive degree, and $i_p^*(\iota_{\xi_M}\beta)=0$: in positive degree because $i_p^*$ kills such forms, and in degree $0$ because $(\iota_{\xi_M}\beta)(p)=\beta_p(\xi_M(p))=0$. Also $i_p^*(d\beta)=0=d(i_p^*\beta)$, since $d\beta$ has positive degree and $d=0$ on a point. So $i_p^*$ commutes with $d_G$ and gives a ring homomorphism
$$i_p^*:H_G(M)\to S(\mathfrak g^*)^G,\qquad \alpha\mapsto\alpha_{[0]}(p),$$
evaluation of the form-degree-$0$ component at $p$. For the equivariant symplectic form $\omega+\mu$ of Notman–Sanabani's Proposition 3.14 it gives $\mu(p)$, the value of the moment map: this is their Lemma 3.16 at an isolated fixed point.

Integration. Let $M$ be compact, oriented, without boundary, of dimension $n$. For $\alpha\in S(\mathfrak g^*)\otimes\Omega(M)$ define $\int_M\alpha\in S(\mathfrak g^*)$ coefficientwise: write $\alpha=\sum_Iq_I\otimes\alpha_I$ with $(q_I)$ a basis of polynomials and set $\int_M\alpha=\sum_Iq_I\int_M(\alpha_I)_{[n]}$, keeping only the top-degree part of each form. Equivalently, $\big(\int_M\alpha\big)(\xi)=\int_M\alpha(\xi)_{[n]}$; Libine integrates in this way, and Notman–Sanabani's Remark 2.80 calls the corresponding push-forward to a point the equivariant integral. Everything rests on the following lemma.

blocks.title: Equivariant Stokes theorem
blocks.body: Let $G$ act on a compact oriented $n$-manifold $M$ without boundary. For every $\beta\in S(\mathfrak g^*)\otimes\Omega(M)$, $\int_Md_G\beta=0$. Consequently integration is well defined on $H_G(M)$, and it is $S(\mathfrak g^*)^G$-linear.

Both sides are polynomials in $\xi$, so it suffices to fix $\xi\in\mathfrak g$ and regard $\beta(\xi)$ as an ordinary form. The top-degree part of $(d_G\beta)(\xi)=d\beta(\xi)-\iota_{\xi_M}\beta(\xi)$ is
$$d\big(\beta(\xi)_{[n-1]}\big)-\iota_{\xi_M}\big(\beta(\xi)_{[n+1]}\big)=d\big(\beta(\xi)_{[n-1]}\big),$$
because there are no $(n+1)$-forms on an $n$-manifold. By Stokes' theorem on the closed manifold $M$, its integral is $0$. So if $\alpha'=\alpha+d_G\beta$, then $\int_M\alpha'=\int_M\alpha$, and $\int_M$ descends to cohomology (Libine's Remark 47 draws the same conclusion for the localisation formula). Linearity over $S(\mathfrak g^*)^G$ is immediate from the coefficientwise definition.

blocks.title: Localisation for a circle action on a surface
blocks.body:
Let the circle $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ act smoothly on a compact connected oriented surface $M$ without boundary by the flow $\varphi_s$ of a vector field $X$ (so $\varphi_{2\pi}=\mathrm{id}$), preserving the orientation, with finite fixed-point set $F$ (the zeros of $X$). Let $d_X=d-u\,\iota_X$ on $\Omega(M)^{S^1}[u]$.

1. At each $p\in F$ there is an integer $w_p\neq0$, the weight at $p$, such that for every $S^1$-invariant inner product on $T_pM$ the map $(d\varphi_s)_p$ is rotation by the angle $w_ps$ in a positively oriented orthonormal basis.
2. For every $d_X$-closed $\alpha=\alpha_{[0]}+\alpha_{[2]}$ of even form degree (coefficients polynomial in $u$),
$$\int_M\alpha=\sum_{p\in F}\frac{2\pi\,\alpha_{[0]}(p)}{u\,w_p}\qquad\text{in }\mathbb{R}[u,u^{-1}].$$
3. $\sum_{p\in F}1/w_p=0$.

This is the two-dimensional case of the Berline–Vergne theorem in Libine's notes (Theorem 46) and of the Atiyah–Bott–Berline–Vergne formula quoted by Notman–Sanabani (Theorem 3.28), which allow higher dimensions (both), a general compact group acting with isolated zeros of the generating field (Libine) and non-isolated fixed components for Hamiltonian torus actions (Notman–Sanabani); the normalisations are compared in the conventions block below.

We follow the strategy of Libine's §7 (an invariant metric, an invariant $1$-form $\theta$ with $\iota_X\theta\ne0$ off the fixed points, exactness of the top-degree part there, and a local model at each fixed point), writing out the surface case in full. Libine takes $\theta_X=g(X,\cdot)$, so that $\iota_X\theta_X=g(X,X)$, and divides by $(d-\iota_X)\theta_X$; on a surface we may instead normalise $\theta$ so that $\iota_X\theta=1$, which makes the division explicit. The text of Libine's proof of his Theorem 46 that we could read stops before the final Stokes step, so Steps 3 and 4 below are our own argument.

Step 1: an invariant metric and the form $\theta$. Average any Riemannian metric $g_0$ over the circle, $g=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi_s^*g_0\,ds$, as in Libine's §7.1; then $\varphi_s^*g=g$ for all $s$. A flow preserves its own generator, $(\varphi_s)_*X=X$. On $M\setminus F$ put $\theta=g(X,\cdot)/g(X,X)$. Then $\varphi_s^*\theta=\theta$, so $L_X\theta=0$, and $\iota_X\theta=1$. By Cartan's formula $\iota_Xd\theta=L_X\theta-d(\iota_X\theta)=0$. On a surface, a $2$-form that vanishes when one slot is filled with a nonzero vector is zero (if $X_q\neq0$, extend it to a basis $X_q,v$ of $T_qM$; then $d\theta(X_q,v)=0$). Hence $d\theta=0$ on $M\setminus F$.

Step 2: the top part is exact off $F$. Write $\alpha_{[0]}=\sum_{k\ge0}u^ka_k$ and $\alpha_{[2]}=\sum_{k\ge0}u^kb_k$ with functions $a_k$ and $2$-forms $b_k$. The odd part of $d_X\alpha$ is $d\alpha_{[0]}-u\,\iota_X\alpha_{[2]}$, so $d_X\alpha=0$ says $da_0=0$ and $da_{k+1}=\iota_Xb_k$ for $k\ge0$. On $M\setminus F$, $\theta\wedge b_k$ is a $3$-form on a surface, hence $0$, so $0=\iota_X(\theta\wedge b_k)=(\iota_X\theta)\,b_k-\theta\wedge\iota_Xb_k$, that is $\theta\wedge\iota_Xb_k=b_k$. Therefore, using $d\theta=0$,
$$d(a_{k+1}\theta)=da_{k+1}\wedge\theta=\iota_Xb_k\wedge\theta=-\theta\wedge\iota_Xb_k=-b_k\qquad\text{on }M\setminus F.$$
This is Libine's Proposition 42 (the top-degree part of a closed equivariant form is exact off the zeros of $X$), with his formula $\alpha=(d-\iota_X)\big(\theta_X\wedge\alpha/(d-\iota_X)\theta_X\big)$ written out in dimension $2$ for the normalised $\theta$, for which $(d-u\,\iota_X)\theta=-u$.

Step 3: the local model at a fixed point. Fix $p\in F$. Each $\varphi_s$ is an isometry of $g$ fixing $p$, so it maps geodesics from $p$ to geodesics from $p$: $\varphi_s(\exp_pv)=\exp_p\big((d\varphi_s)_pv\big)$. Thus $s\mapsto(d\varphi_s)_p$ is a continuous homomorphism from $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ to the orientation-preserving isometries of $(T_pM,g_p)$, that is to $SO(2)$, and every such homomorphism is $s\mapsto$ rotation by $w_ps$ with $w_p\in\mathbb{Z}$. If $w_p=0$, every point $\exp_pv$ near $p$ would be fixed, contradicting that $p$ is isolated; so $w_p\ne0$. (The angle of an orientation-preserving rotation $R$ of an oriented Euclidean plane is determined by $R$ alone: its cosine is $\frac12\operatorname{tr}R$, and the sign of its sine is positive exactly when $(v,Rv)$ is a positive basis for some, equivalently every, $v\neq0$ not fixed by $R$. So any invariant inner product gives the same angles $w_ps$, which proves item 1. Libine's Lemma 45, the invertibility of the linearised action, is the higher-dimensional version of $w_p\neq0$.)

For small $\varepsilon>0$ let $D_\varepsilon(p)=\exp_p\{|v|<\varepsilon\}$, a disc containing no other fixed point, and $C_\varepsilon(p)$ its boundary circle with the boundary orientation of the disc, which is counterclockwise in the oriented chart $\exp_p$. By the formula above, $C_\varepsilon(p)$ is an orbit: for $q\in C_\varepsilon(p)$, $s\mapsto\varphi_s(q)$, $0\le s\le2\pi/|w_p|$, runs once around it, counterclockwise if $w_p>0$ and clockwise if $w_p<0$, with velocity $X$. Since $\theta(X)=1$, for a continuous function $f$
$$\oint_{C_\varepsilon(p)}f\,\theta=\operatorname{sign}(w_p)\int_0^{2\pi/|w_p|}f(\varphi_s(q))\,ds .$$
In particular $\oint_{C_\varepsilon(p)}\theta=2\pi/w_p$, and
$$\Big|\oint_{C_\varepsilon(p)}f\,\theta-\frac{2\pi f(p)}{w_p}\Big|\le\frac{2\pi}{|w_p|}\max_{C_\varepsilon(p)}|f-f(p)|\longrightarrow0\quad(\varepsilon\to0).$$

Step 4: Stokes. Let $M_\varepsilon=M\setminus\bigcup_{p\in F}D_\varepsilon(p)$, a compact surface whose boundary is $\bigsqcup_pC_\varepsilon(p)$ with the opposite orientation. By Step 2 and Stokes' theorem,
$$\int_{M_\varepsilon}b_k=-\int_{M_\varepsilon}d(a_{k+1}\theta)=\sum_{p\in F}\oint_{C_\varepsilon(p)}a_{k+1}\theta .$$
As $\varepsilon\to0$ the left side tends to $\int_Mb_k$ (the discs shrink and $b_k$ is smooth on $M$), and the right side to $\sum_p2\pi a_{k+1}(p)/w_p$ by Step 3. In the same way $0=\int_{M_\varepsilon}d\theta=-\sum_p\oint_{C_\varepsilon(p)}\theta=-2\pi\sum_p1/w_p$, which is item 3. Finally $a_0$ is a closed function on the connected $M$, hence a constant, and
$$\int_M\alpha=\sum_{k\ge0}u^k\int_Mb_k=\sum_{p\in F}\frac{2\pi}{w_p}\sum_{k\ge0}u^ka_{k+1}(p)=\sum_{p\in F}\frac{2\pi\big(\alpha_{[0]}(p)-a_0\big)}{u\,w_p}=\sum_{p\in F}\frac{2\pi\,\alpha_{[0]}(p)}{u\,w_p},$$
the $a_0$ terms cancelling by item 3. If $F$ is empty the same argument (with $M_\varepsilon=M$) gives $\int_M\alpha=0$.

blocks.title: Localisation on the rotating sphere, degree by degree
blocks.body: For the rotation of $S^2$ in the earlier example ($X=\partial_\varphi$, $\mu=d\varphi\wedge dz$, and $\mu+uz$ equivariantly closed), find the weights at the poles and check the localisation theorem for $\alpha=(\mu+uz)^k$, $k\ge0$. Which of these classes does the formula show to be nonzero, and what does it say about the others?
blocks.solution:
Near the north pole the chart $(x,y)$ is positively oriented (the outward normal there is $+\partial_z$), and $X=x\,\partial_y-y\,\partial_x$ rotates it counterclockwise at unit speed, so $w_N=1$. Near the south pole the outward normal is $-\partial_z$, so $(x,y)$ is negatively oriented there and $(y,x)$ is positively oriented; in that chart the same field rotates clockwise, so $w_S=-1$. As item 3 requires, $1/w_N+1/w_S=0$.

Since $\mu\wedge\mu=0$, the binomial theorem gives $(\mu+uz)^k=u^kz^k+k\,u^{k-1}z^{k-1}\mu$, so $\alpha_{[0]}=u^kz^k$ and $\alpha_{[2]}=ku^{k-1}z^{k-1}\mu$. For $k\ge1$,
$$\int_{S^2}\alpha=k\,u^{k-1}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{-1}^1z^{k-1}\,dz\,d\varphi=2\pi u^{k-1}\big(1-(-1)^k\big),$$
and for $k=0$ the integral is $0$. The fixed-point side is
$$\frac{2\pi u^k\cdot1^k}{u\cdot1}+\frac{2\pi u^k(-1)^k}{u\cdot(-1)}=2\pi u^{k-1}\big(1-(-1)^k\big),$$
which agrees for every $k$, including $k=0$. For $k=1$ this is the area $4\pi$, obtained from the values $\pm1$ of the moment map at the two poles, which is the computation of Notman–Sanabani's §1.2. Since $\int$ is defined on $H_{S^1}(S^2)$, the classes $(\mu+uz)^k$ with $k$ odd are nonzero. For even $k$ both sides vanish, so $\int_{S^2}(\mu+uz)^{2j}=0$; this says nothing about whether the class is zero. In fact it is not: $(\mu+uz)^2$ and $u^2$ have the same restrictions to both poles (exercise 5 below), and $u^2\ne0$ in $H_{S^1}(S^2)$ because its restriction to a pole is $u^2\ne0$ in $H_{S^1}(\mathrm{pt})$. Integration detects only part of a class.

blocks.title: Normalising the localisation formula
blocks.body: The same theorem appears with different constants. Before using a formula from a paper, test it on the rotating sphere, whose area $4\pi$ must come out of two poles with opposite weights.

rows.text: $d_X=d-u\,\iota_X$, $X$ the velocity field of a $2\pi$-periodic flow, integer weights $w_p$ read in positively oriented charts; on a surface $\int_M\alpha=\sum_p2\pi\,\alpha_{[0]}(p)/(u\,w_p)$.

$d_{eq}=d-\iota_X$ (Definition 16), generating fields defined through $\exp(-tX)$; Theorem 46: $\int_M\alpha(X)=(-2\pi)^{\dim M/2}\sum_p\alpha(X)_{[0]}(p)/\det^{1/2}(L(X,p))$, with $\det^{1/2}$ the Pfaffian $c_1\cdots c_{n/2}$ of his local model $L_X=\sum_jc_j(x_{2j}\partial_{2j-1}-x_{2j-1}\partial_{2j})$. Read in terms of the vector field itself: on a surface $L_X=-c\,(x_1\partial_2-x_2\partial_1)$, so a field rotating counterclockwise with speed $w$ has $c=-w$, and $-2\pi/c=2\pi/w$ agrees with this page.

Theorem 3.28: $\int_M\overline\omega(X)=\sum_F\int_F\iota_F^*\overline\omega(X)/e^T(
u_F,X)$ with $e^T(
u_F,X)=\prod_j ig(c_1(
u_{F,j})+ eta_{F,j}(X) ig)$ (Remark 3.25), which at an isolated fixed point is the product of the weights $ eta_{F,j}(X)$ (Remark 3.26). No $2\pi$ is written; in their §1.2 example the generator is taken to be $X=-2\pi\,\partial_	heta$.

Theorem 9.1 sums over fixed components with the equivariant Euler form, normalised through $\det^{1/2}(\zeta/2\pi)$ (eq. (32)); his isolated-point and Duistermaat–Heckman formulas (Remark 9.4, eq. (51)) carry a sign $(-1)^{\dim M/2}$ and no explicit $2\pi$, and his generating fields use $\exp(-t\xi)$.

blocks.body: Orientations and the sign of the generator enter every localisation computation, and printed examples are not always internally consistent, so recompute them. In spherical coordinates with polar angle $\phi$ and azimuth $\theta$, the outward-oriented area form of the unit sphere is $\sin\phi\,d\phi\wedge d\theta$: at a point of the equator, (outward normal, $\partial_\phi$, $\partial_\theta$) is a positive basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$. So $\int_{S^2}\sin\phi\,d\theta\wedge d\phi=-4\pi$ as an integral of a form. Notman–Sanabani's §1.2 writes the area of the sphere as $\int_{S^2}\sin\phi\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$ over $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $0\le\phi\le\pi$ and obtains $4\pi$ from the localisation formula as $2\pi-(-2\pi)$; read as the integral of a $2$-form on the outward-oriented sphere, that integrand gives $-4\pi$. The same section prints $\iota_X\omega=2\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi=d(2\pi\cos\phi)$ for $X=-2\pi\partial_\theta$, although $d(2\pi\cos\phi)=-2\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi$. If $\omega$ is taken to be the printed integrand $\sin\phi\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$, then $\iota_X\omega=-2\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi$ and the moment map $2\pi\cos\phi$ is right; if $\omega$ is the outward area form $\sin\phi\,d\phi\wedge d\theta$, then $\iota_X\omega=2\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi$ and the moment map is $-2\pi\cos\phi$. The final answer survives, but a reader who copies one line at a time gets a sign wrong.

1. Show that the restriction map $i_p^*$ to a fixed point is a ring homomorphism $H_G(M)\to S(\mathfrak g^*)^G$, and compute it on $\mu+uz\in H_{S^1}(S^2)$ at both poles.
2. Let the circle act on $S^2$ by $\varphi_s$ = rotation about the $z$-axis by the angle $ms$, with $m$ a nonzero integer. Find $X$, a function $f$ with $\mu+uf$ equivariantly closed, the weights at the poles, and check the localisation theorem for $(\mu+uf)^k$.
3. Use item 3 of the theorem to show that a circle action on a compact connected oriented surface with finitely many fixed points cannot have exactly one fixed point.
4. On $M\setminus F$, with $\theta$ as in Step 1, show that $d_X\theta=-u$ and that $\alpha=d_X\big(-u^{-1}\theta\,\alpha\big)$ for every $d_X$-closed even $\alpha$, with coefficients in $\mathbb{R}[u,u^{-1}]$. Explain why this does not make $\alpha$ exact on $M$, and compare with Libine's formula $\alpha=(d-\iota_X)\big(\theta\wedge\alpha/(d-\iota_X)\theta\big)$.
5. With $m=1$ in exercise 2, show that $(\mu+uz)^2-u^2$ restricts to $0$ at both poles, deduce from the theorem that $\int_{S^2}\big((\mu+uz)^2-u^2\big)(\mu+uz)^j=0$ for every $j\ge0$, and verify this directly.

blocks.title: Algebraic de Rham cohomology and periods
blocks.body:
Arithmetic geometers use a version of de Rham cohomology built from algebraic differential forms. For a smooth variety $X$ over a field $K$ (see [[algebraic-varieties]]), the algebraic de Rham complex $\Omega^\bullet_{X/K}$ consists of the sheaves of algebraic (Kähler) differential forms with the algebraic $d$, and $H^n_{dR}(X/K)$ is its hypercohomology (nLab; for singular varieties Grothendieck's more subtle definition is needed). When $X$ is affine, hypercohomology is simply the cohomology of the complex of global algebraic forms.

For $K\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ and $X$ smooth projective, Grothendieck's comparison theorem, which Kreutz–Shen–Vial cite through GAGA and the analytic Poincaré lemma, gives a canonical isomorphism
$$H^n_{dR}(X/K)\otimes_K\mathbb{C}\cong H^n_B(X^{an},\mathbb{Q})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{C},$$
where $H_B$ is singular (Betti) cohomology of the complex manifold $X^{an}$; over $\mathbb{C}$ this is de Rham's theorem with Dolbeault's theorem, as Kedlaya explains. The two sides carry different rational structures: a $K$-structure from algebraic forms and a $\mathbb{Q}$-structure from integral cycles. The entries of the matrix of the comparison isomorphism in such bases are the periods $\int_\gamma\omega$ of algebraic forms over rational cycles. Kedlaya adds that the Hodge filtration descends to $K$ while the Hodge decomposition does not, and that in characteristic $p$ the Poincaré lemma fails ("too many constants": $d(f^p)=0$), which is one starting point for crystalline and prismatic cohomology. Dolbeault cohomology and the Hodge decomposition $d=\partial+\bar\partial$ are not covered here; see Lim, §2.2 to §2.3, and [[hodge-theory]].

blocks.title: The multiplicative group and its period
blocks.body: Let $X=\mathbb{G}_m=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}[z,z^{-1}]$, the affine line minus the origin over $\mathbb{Q}$. Compute $H^*_{dR}(X/\mathbb{Q})$ from global algebraic forms, compute the period of the generator over the unit circle, and explain the role of the twist $\mathbb{Q}(1)$. What changes in characteristic $p$?
blocks.solution: Global functions are Laurent polynomials $\sum a_nz^n$ and global $1$-forms are $f\,dz$ with $f$ a Laurent polynomial. Since $d(z^n)=nz^{n-1}dz$, the image of $d$ contains $z^m\,dz$ for every $m\ne-1$ and nothing involving $z^{-1}dz$. So $H^1_{dR}(X/\mathbb{Q})=\mathbb{Q}\cdot[dz/z]$, and $H^0=\mathbb{Q}$ (the kernel of $d$ is the constants, since $nz^{n-1}=0$ forces $n=0$ in characteristic $0$). The complex points form $\mathbb{C}^\times$, homotopy equivalent to the circle, and the period of $dz/z$ over the unit circle is $\int_0^{2\pi}i\,dt=2\pi i$. So the comparison isomorphism identifies the $\mathbb{Q}$-line spanned by $[dz/z]$ with $2\pi i$ times the rational Betti line, which is why de Rham classes are compared with Betti classes twisted by $\mathbb{Q}(1)=2\pi i\,\mathbb{Q}$; in degree $2k$ the twist is $\mathbb{Q}(k)$, as in Kreutz–Shen–Vial. In characteristic $p$ the same computation over $\mathbb{F}_p$ gives $d(z^{p})=pz^{p-1}dz=0$, so $z^p$ is a non-constant closed $0$-form and $z^{p-1}dz$ is no longer exact: $H^0$ and $H^1$ become infinite dimensional, the failure of the Poincaré lemma that Kedlaya describes.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $H^*_{dR}$ of the affine line $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}[z]$ and of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Q}[z,(z-1)^{-1},z^{-1}]$ (the line minus two points), and the periods of the generators over small circles.
2. Over $\mathbb{F}_p$, find a basis of $H^1$ of the complex $\mathbb{F}_p[z]\xrightarrow{d}\mathbb{F}_p[z]\,dz$.
3. Show that the period of $dz/(z^2+1)$ over a small loop around $i$ in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{\pm i\}$ is $\pi$, by writing $\frac1{z^2+1}=\frac1{2i}\big(\frac1{z-i}-\frac1{z+i}\big)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and using the period $2\pi i$ of $dz/(z-i)$.

blocks.title: De Rham–Betti classes and the period criterion
blocks.body:
Kreutz–Shen–Vial package the comparison isomorphism into triples
$$H^n_{dRB}(X,\mathbb{Q}(k))=\big(H^n_{dR}(X/K),\ H^n_B(X^{an},\mathbb{Q}(k)),\ c^n_X\big),$$
where $\mathbb{Q}(k)=(2\pi i)^k\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{C}$ and $H^n_B(X^{an},\mathbb{Q}(k))=H^n_B(X^{an},\mathbb{Q})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{Q}(k)$, a $\mathbb{Q}$-subspace of $H^n_B(X^{an},\mathbb{C})$. A de Rham–Betti class is a pair $(\alpha_{dR},\alpha_B)$ with $c_X(\alpha_{dR}\otimes1)=\alpha_B\otimes1$; letting $\alpha_B$ have coefficients in a field $L'$ with $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq L'\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ gives their $L'$-de Rham–Betti classes (Definitions 2.1 and 2.3, in the language of an abstract category of such triples). The basic examples are cycle classes: for an algebraic cycle $Z$ of codimension $k$, the de Rham and Betti cycle classes of $Z$ correspond under $c^{2k}_X$, up to a sign (their equation (2) and the sentence before it). The paper's conjectures ask whether every de Rham–Betti class is of this kind.

Whether a given de Rham class is part of such a pair is a statement about its periods. To see this one needs only how $c_X$ looks to a homology class. By de Rham's theorem and the universal coefficient theorem over a field, a complex Betti class is the same as a homomorphism $H_n(X^{an};\mathbb{Q})\to\mathbb{C}$, and $c_X$ sends the class of $\omega$ to $\gamma\mapsto\int_\gamma\omega$: this is how the paper defines the periods of $X$, and how the comparison was described in the previous section (for affine $X$, as for $\mathbb{G}_m$, $\omega$ is literally a closed holomorphic form on $X^{an}$). We take this description of $c_X$ as given. The paper's remark after its equation (2), made there 'by Poincaré duality', then becomes the following elementary statement (the paper asks for the normalised periods to lie in the base field $K$; the argument works for any subfield $L\subseteq\mathbb{C}$).

blocks.title: Period criterion for de Rham–Betti classes
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $K\subseteq\mathbb{C}$, let $L\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be a subfield, and let $\omega\in H^n_{dR}(X/K)$. There is $\beta\in H^n_B(X^{an},\mathbb{Q})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}(2\pi i)^kL$ with $c_X(\omega\otimes1)=\beta$ if and only if
$$\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^k}\int_\gamma\omega\in L\qquad\text{for every }\gamma\in H_n(X^{an};\mathbb{Q}),$$
and it suffices to test $\gamma$ in a basis of $H_n(X^{an};\mathbb{Q})$. The class $\beta$ is then unique.

$X^{an}$ is a compact manifold, so $H_n(X^{an};\mathbb{Q})$ is finite dimensional; let $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_m$ be a basis. By the universal coefficient theorem over a field, $H^n_B(X^{an};F)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}\big(H_n(X^{an};\mathbb{Q}),F\big)$ for $F=\mathbb{Q}$ and $F=\mathbb{C}$, compatibly with $\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{C}$. Let $\gamma^1,\dots,\gamma^m$ be the dual basis of $H^n_B(X^{an};\mathbb{Q})$. Every complex class is uniquely $\sum_jc_j\gamma^j$ with $c_j\in\mathbb{C}$ its value on $\gamma_j$, and the subspace $H^n_B(X^{an},\mathbb{Q})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}(2\pi i)^kL$ consists exactly of the classes with all $c_j\in(2\pi i)^kL$, because the $\gamma^j$ form a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis. For $c_X(\omega\otimes1)$ the coefficients are $c_j=\int_{\gamma_j}\omega$. This proves the criterion for basis elements and the uniqueness of $\beta$; for an arbitrary rational $\gamma=\sum_jq_j\gamma_j$ the period is $\sum_jq_j\int_{\gamma_j}\omega$, and $L\supseteq\mathbb{Q}$ is closed under such combinations.

blocks.title: Periods of an elliptic curve and Legendre's relation
blocks.body: Kreutz–Shen–Vial's first example: for an elliptic curve $E$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, $H^1_{dR}(E/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ is spanned by the classes of $\omega=dx/y$ and of the second-kind form $\eta=x\,dx/y$, and for a basis $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ of $H_1(E^{an};\mathbb{Q})$ the four periods $\omega_j=\int_{\gamma_j}\omega$, $\eta_j=\int_{\gamma_j}\eta$ satisfy Legendre's relation in the form $\omega_1\eta_2-\omega_2\eta_1\in\mathbb{Q}^\times\cdot2\pi i$. Prove this for the Weierstrass curve $y^2=4x^3-g_2x-g_3$ of a lattice $\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}\Omega_1+\mathbb{Z}\Omega_2$ with $\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_2/\Omega_1)>0$, show that the number is then exactly $2\pi i$, and explain why $\eta$, which has a pole, defines a class in the de Rham cohomology of the compact surface $E^{an}$. Then recover the same number from the wedge pairing on the torus.
blocks.solution:
Setup. The Weierstrass function $\wp$ of $\Lambda$ (Pastras (1.18)) is $\Lambda$-periodic with double poles exactly at $\Lambda$, is even, and satisfies $\wp'^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3$ (Pastras (1.28)). The zeta function is defined by $\zeta'=-\wp$ with $\zeta(z)-1/z\to0$ at $0$ (Pastras (2.1)-(2.2)); it is meromorphic with a simple pole of residue $1$ at each lattice point. The function $\zeta(z+\Omega_j)-\zeta(z)$ has derivative $-\wp(z+\Omega_j)+\wp(z)=0$, so it is a constant $H_j$, the quasi-period (Pastras (2.5), with full periods $\Omega_j=2\omega_j$ and $H_j=2\zeta(\omega_j)$ in his half-period notation). We use the standard fact that $z\mapsto(\wp(z),\wp'(z))$ identifies $(\mathbb{C}/\Lambda)\setminus\{0\}$ with the affine curve, so that $E^{an}$ is the torus $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ and
$$\frac{dx}{y}=\frac{\wp'(z)\,dz}{\wp'(z)}=dz,\qquad\frac{x\,dx}{y}=\wp(z)\,dz .$$
Choose a base point $a$ with no lattice point on the boundary of the parallelogram $P$ with vertices $a,\ a+\Omega_1,\ a+\Omega_1+\Omega_2,\ a+\Omega_2$, and let $\gamma_j$ be the image of the segment from $a$ to $a+\Omega_j$. Under the linear isomorphism $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{C}$, $e_j\mapsto\Omega_j$, these are the two standard circles of the torus, so they form a basis of $H_1(E^{an};\mathbb{Z})$. Then $\omega_j=\int_a^{a+\Omega_j}dz=\Omega_j$ and $\eta_j=\int_a^{a+\Omega_j}\wp\,dz=-\big(\zeta(a+\Omega_j)-\zeta(a)\big)=-H_j$.

Legendre's relation by residues. This is the proof that the Wikipedia article on Legendre's relation describes (integrate $\zeta$ around a fundamental region) and that Pastras carries out for (2.7). The hypothesis $\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_2/\Omega_1)>0$ means that $a\to a+\Omega_1\to a+\Omega_1+\Omega_2\to a+\Omega_2\to a$ runs around $P$ counterclockwise. Pairing opposite sides,
$$\oint_{\partial P}\zeta\,dz=\int_a^{a+\Omega_1}\big(\zeta(z)-\zeta(z+\Omega_2)\big)dz+\int_a^{a+\Omega_2}\big(\zeta(z+\Omega_1)-\zeta(z)\big)dz=-H_2\Omega_1+H_1\Omega_2 .$$
$P$ contains exactly one point of $\Lambda$, where $\zeta$ has residue $1$, so the residue theorem gives $H_1\Omega_2-H_2\Omega_1=2\pi i$; in Pastras's half-periods this is his $\omega_2\zeta(\omega_1)-\omega_1\zeta(\omega_2)=\pi i/2$ multiplied by $4$. In the paper's notation,
$$\omega_1\eta_2-\omega_2\eta_1=-\Omega_1H_2+\Omega_2H_1=2\pi i .$$
For another equation, such as $y'^2=x^3-ax-b$, put $y=2y'$: then $y^2=4x^3-4ax-4b$ is of Weierstrass form, the forms $dx/y'$ and $x\,dx/y'$ are $2\,dx/y$ and $2x\,dx/y$, and the combination becomes $4\cdot2\pi i$, still a nonzero rational multiple of $2\pi i$.

The class of $\eta$. The form $\wp\,dz$ is holomorphic, hence closed, on $E\setminus\{0\}$: $d(f\,dz)=\partial_{\bar z}f\,d\bar z\wedge dz=0$ for holomorphic $f$. Its residue at $0$ is $0$ because $\wp$ is even. Let $\chi$ be a smooth function on $E$ equal to $1$ near $0$ and supported in a small disc $D$ around $0$, and put
$$\tilde\eta=\wp\,dz+d(\chi\zeta)\quad\text{on }E\setminus\{0\}.$$
Near $0$, $\tilde\eta=\wp\,dz+\zeta'\,dz=0$, so $\tilde\eta$ extends to a smooth closed $1$-form on $E$; outside $D$ it equals $\wp\,dz$. Choosing $a$ so that the $\gamma_j$ avoid $D$, $\int_{\gamma_j}\tilde\eta=\eta_j$, and by the theorem that periods determine classes, $[\tilde\eta]\in H^1_{dR}(E;\mathbb{C})$ is the unique class with periods $\eta_1,\eta_2$. Another cutoff $\chi'$ changes $\tilde\eta$ by $d\big((\chi'-\chi)\zeta\big)$, where $(\chi'-\chi)\zeta$ is smooth because $\chi'-\chi$ vanishes near $0$; so the class is independent of $\chi$. The pole is harmless precisely because its residue vanishes: a loop around $0$ has period $2\pi i\operatorname{res}_0=0$.

The same number from the pairing. Use real coordinates $z=x_1\Omega_1+x_2\Omega_2$ with $x_j\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$; since $(\Omega_1,\Omega_2)$ is a positively oriented real basis of $\mathbb{C}$, $(x_1,x_2)$ are oriented coordinates and $\int_Edx_1\wedge dx_2=1$. A closed $1$-form $\alpha$ with periods $A_j=\int_{\gamma_j}\alpha$ is $A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2+df$ (periods determine classes), so for closed $\alpha,\beta$
$$\int_E\alpha\wedge\beta=A_1(\alpha)A_2(\beta)-A_2(\alpha)A_1(\beta),$$
the exact parts contributing $0$ by Stokes, as in the torus computations of the Poincaré duality section. Hence $\int_Edz\wedge\tilde\eta=\omega_1\eta_2-\omega_2\eta_1$. Directly: $dz\wedge\wp\,dz=0$ and $dz\wedge d(\chi\zeta)=-d(\chi\zeta\,dz)$ on $E\setminus\{0\}$, so with $D_\varepsilon$ a small disc around $0$ (where $\chi=1$),
$$\int_Edz\wedge\tilde\eta=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\Big(-\int_{E\setminus D_\varepsilon}d(\chi\zeta\,dz)\Big)=\oint_{\partial D_\varepsilon}\zeta\,dz=2\pi i,$$
because $\partial(E\setminus D_\varepsilon)$ is $\partial D_\varepsilon$ with the reversed orientation. The two computations agree: Legendre's relation says that the wedge pairing of the two de Rham classes is $2\pi i$, the period of $\mathbb{Q}(1)$, consistent with the twist $\mathbb{Q}(1)$ that the paper attaches to $H^2$.

blocks.title: Closed forms in physics
blocks.body:
Bhardwaj et al.'s lectures on generalised symmetries assume this page's material under a physics dictionary. Spacetime is a $d$-manifold.
- A conserved current for a continuous symmetry is a closed $(d-1)$-form $j$ (the Hodge dual of a divergence-free vector current); for a $p$-form symmetry it is a closed $(d-p-1)$-form.
- The symmetry operator on a closed oriented submanifold $\Sigma$ is $U_g(\Sigma)=\exp\big(i\alpha\int_\Sigma j\big)$. It is topological: deforming $\Sigma$ to $\Sigma'$ with $\Sigma-\Sigma'=\partial\Sigma_d$ changes the exponent by $\int_{\Sigma_d}dj=0$. So charges are periods of closed forms, and only the homology class of $\Sigma$ matters.
- In Maxwell theory $F=dA$ locally, the Bianchi identity $dF=0$ gives a magnetic symmetry with current $F$, and the equation of motion $d\star F=0$ an electric one with current $\star F$. Gauge transformations shift $A$ by exact forms, $A\mapsto A-\frac{1}{2\pi}d\theta$ in their normalisation, which leave $F$ unchanged.
- Fluxes through closed surfaces are quantised: in their normalisation $\int_{S^2}F=q\in\mathbb{Z}$ around an 't Hooft line, so $[F]$ is an integral class in the sense of the de Rham section, and the field of a monopole is a closed, non-exact form on the complement of its worldline, like $\Phi$ above.
- A charged defect on $M_p$ appears in the conservation law as $dj=q\,\delta(M_p)$, the Poincaré dual delta-form; linking of $\Sigma$ with $M_p$ then gives the phase $e^{iq\alpha}$ by Stokes.
- In discrete gauge theories, forms are replaced by cochains and wedge products by cup products, with actions such as $2\pi\int a\cup\delta b$, the cochain analogue of $B\wedge dA$.

blocks.title: Charge measured on any enclosing surface
blocks.body: In $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ (a time slice), a static point charge at the origin gives the electric flux form $\star E=\frac{q}{4\pi}\Phi$ with $\Phi$ from the flux example. Show that the charge measured by $\int_\Sigma\star E$ is $q$ for every closed surface $\Sigma$ enclosing the origin once (homologous to the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$) and $0$ for surfaces not enclosing it, and phrase the source equation with a delta-form.
blocks.solution: $\Phi$ is closed on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, and $H_2(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\})=\mathbb{Z}$ is generated by the unit sphere $S$. If $\Sigma$ is homologous to $S$, then $\Sigma-S=\partial c$ for a $3$-chain $c$ avoiding the origin, and $\int_\Sigma\Phi-\int_S\Phi=\int_cd\Phi=0$, so $\int_\Sigma\star E=\frac q{4\pi}4\pi=q$. A surface not enclosing the origin bounds in $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, so the integral is $0$. On all of $\mathbb{R}^3$, $d\star E$ is not zero but concentrated at the origin: $d\star E=q\,\delta^3(x)$, where $\delta^3$ is the $3$-form Poincaré dual to the point (the delta function times $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$), and Stokes on a ball $B$ around the origin gives $\int_{\partial B}\star E=\int_Bq\,\delta^3=q$, the same answer.

blocks.body:
1. In $\mathbb{R}^3$, the magnetic field of a steady current along the $z$-axis is represented by the $1$-form $\frac{I}{2\pi}d\varphi$ (angle around the axis) for the field $B$ itself. Show that it is closed but not exact on the complement of the axis, and compute its period on a loop around the axis.
2. Show that if $A$ and $A'$ are two potentials for the same $F$ on a manifold $M$, then $A'-A$ is closed, and that it is exact if $H^1(M)=0$; describe the extra possible gauge fields on $S^1\times\mathbb{R}^3$.
3. Explain why the charge operator $U_g(\Sigma)$ depends only on $[\Sigma]\in H_{d-1}$ of the complement of the charged operators.
